# Universal elementary schooling (`universal_schooling`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, printing_press, vernacular_translation, paper
- Core idea: Every child, girls included, is taught reading, writing and arithmetic in the spoken language for a few years, free of charge and by obligation. Literacy pays off for the whole society (soldiers who read orders, farmers who read almanacs, craftsmen who calculate) but not enough for a poor family to give up a child's labour, so it has to be compulsory, free and fitted around the farming year. What is needed: a school within walking distance, a paid and trained teacher, a cheap printed primer, local funding by a fixed tax, and inspection. Where teachers are scarce, let older pupils teach younger ones (monitorial method).
- Pitfalls:
  - Decreeing schools without teachers, pay or books: Prussia's 1717 edict and the Ming order of 1375 were patchily obeyed for generations
  - Teaching in Latin, classical Chinese or another learned language instead of the mother tongue
  - Ignoring that parents need children's work: allow harvest holidays and half-days or the benches stay empty
  - Expecting the powerful to welcome it: many landlords, employers and clergy held that literate peasants and servants become insolent
  - Promising quick wealth: the returns take a generation
- History: china: 124 BC – Imperial Academy for future officials; 1375 the Hongwu emperor orders community schools (shexue) in every village, with uneven results; india: village schools (pathshalas) and monastic teaching existed for centuries; state mass schooling only from the 19th–20th c.; greece: Sparta's compulsory state upbringing of boys (agoge); Hellenistic cities such as Teos (3rd c. BC) fund teachers for all free children; rome: c. AD 64 – Joshua ben Gamla is credited with ordering teachers for children in every Judaean town (Talmud, Bava Batra 21a); islamic: from 7th–8th c. – Quran schools (kuttab) teach boys reading and writing widely, by fee or endowment, without compulsion; americas: 15th c. – Mexica (Aztec) boys and girls of all ranks are expected to attend a school (telpochcalli or calmecac); coverage in practice uncertain; 1647 Massachusetts requires towns to keep schools; europe: 1524 – Luther urges town councils to found schools for boys and girls; 1559 Württemberg school ordinance; 1592 Pfalz-Zweibrücken makes schooling compulsory for both sexes; 1717 and 1763 Prussia; 1774 Austria; 1881–1882 France free, compulsory and secular; east_asia: 17th–19th c. – Japanese temple schools (terakoya) give wide literacy without compulsion; 1872 compulsory schooling decreed
